gbs333-aa4852-d1e107.summary: States the question: whether every attribute (passio) is demonstrable of its first subject.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e118.summary: Methodological note: this question and the two following are merely incidental (logical side-issues) and will therefore be treated briefly, by notabilia followed by responsive conclusions.
claims: Questions 4–6 are incidental to the main inquiry and will be treated summarily.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e132.summary: Defines the first subject of a predicate: that to which the predicate can belong with everything else excluded, and to which nothing else can belong once that subject is excluded. Illustrates with 'capable of learning' (disciplinabile): both man and the intellective soul are subjects of it, but the intellective soul is the first subject, since the predicate belongs to the soul even when separated from everything else, and to nothing once the soul is removed, whereas it is not removed from the soul when man is destroyed.
claims: The first subject of a predicate is that to which it can belong with all else abstracted and to which alone it belongs.
The intellective soul, not man, is the first subject of 'capable of learning'.
Capacity for learning belongs to the soul even when separated from the body.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e167.summary: Gives Ockham's alternative definition from his logic (Summa logicae): a subject is first when the predicate does not belong universally to something superior or disparate to it first. Biel draws the consequence that a first subject need not be convertible with its attribute (e.g. intellective soul and 'capable of learning', heat and 'heat-producing'), though perhaps every convertible subject is first, and judges the first description clearer.
claims: On Ockham's logical definition, a subject is first when the predicate does not belong first and universally to something superior or disparate.
Not every first subject is convertible with its attribute.
Perhaps every convertible subject is a first subject.
The first definition is clearer than Ockham's.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e193.summary: Second notandum: attributes are of four kinds: those signifying an absolute inhering form, those signifying motion or change, those connoting something extrinsic affirmatively, and those connoting something negatively or privatively. What an attribute connotes is what its abstract form principally signifies.
claims: Attributes are fourfold: absolute inhering form, motion or change, extrinsic affirmative connotation, negative or privative connotation.
An attribute connotes what its abstract term principally signifies.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e213.summary: Third notandum: sometimes there is a middle between the first subject and the attribute, to which the attribute belongs prior (i.e., more evidently); sometimes there is none, namely when the attribute belongs to nothing more evidently, and then the proposition predicating it of that subject is immediate.
claims: Sometimes a middle exists between first subject and attribute, to which the attribute belongs more evidently.
When no such middle exists, the proposition predicating the attribute of the first subject is immediate.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e237.summary: Raises an objection to the third notandum: a middle between a first subject and its attribute seems contradictory. If a is the first subject, c the attribute, and b the middle, then b is subject of c (since the middle is subject in the major premise) and prior to a, so a would not be the first subject.
claims: Objection: if a middle b stands between first subject a and attribute c, b is a prior subject of c, so a is not first.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e259.summary: Resolves the objection by distinguishing senses of 'subject': here it means not the subject of any proposition but the subject of an attribute, a complex term of which the attribute is predicated accidentally and convertibly. So there can be a first subject with no prior subject mediating, while there is still a middle that is not itself a subject in this sense, namely a definition.
claims: 'Subject' in the definition of first subject means subject of the attribute, not subject of a proposition.
A first subject can have a middle that is not itself a subject of the attribute, such as a definition.
concepts: subject of a proposition vs. subject of an attribute

gbs333-aa4852-d1e282.summary: First conclusion, drawing on the third notandum: attributes with no middle between them and their first subject cannot be demonstrated of it, because an immediate proposition is indemonstrable; attributes that do have such a middle are demonstrable of their first subject. Which attributes have a middle is settled by the following conclusions.
claims: Attributes with no middle between them and their first subject are not demonstrable of it.
Immediate propositions are indemonstrable.
Attributes with a middle are demonstrable of their first subject.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e304.summary: Second conclusion: an attribute signifying an absolute inhering form is not demonstrable of its first subject; such an attribute is known of its first subject through experience.
claims: Attributes signifying an absolute inhering form are not demonstrable of their first subject.
Such attributes are known of their first subject by experience.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e315.summary: Third conclusion: such an attribute (signifying an absolute inhering form) is demonstrable of a non-first subject through the first subject as middle.
claims: An attribute signifying an absolute form can be demonstrated of a non-first subject by using the first subject as middle term.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e324.summary: Fourth conclusion: among attributes of the third kind (connoting something extrinsic affirmatively), some are demonstrable of their first subject and some are not. 'Heat-producing' is not demonstrable of heat; 'having three angles equal to two right angles' is demonstrable of the triangle, and 'corruptible' of composite substance.
claims: Some extrinsic-connoting attributes are demonstrable of their first subject and some are not.
'Heat-producing' is not demonstrable of heat.
'Having three angles equal to two right angles' is demonstrable of the triangle; 'corruptible' of composite substance.

gbs333-aa4852-d1e340.summary: Fifth conclusion: a negative attribute whose opposite is demonstrable of some first subject can be demonstrated, as in the syllogism 'every corruptible is a body; no simple substance is a body; therefore no simple substance is corruptible'.
claims: A negative attribute is demonstrable when its opposite is demonstrable of some first subject.
Incorruptibility of simple substance can be demonstrated from the corporeality of everything corruptible.

gbs333-aa4852.summary: Quaestio 4, the first of three incidental logical questions treated briefly, asks whether every attribute (passio) is demonstrable of its first subject. Biel defines the first subject by an abstraction test (with Ockham's logical definition as an alternative), noting that a first subject need not be convertible with its attribute; divides attributes into four kinds (absolute inhering form, motion, affirmative extrinsic connotation, negative or privative connotation); and observes that a middle sometimes stands between first subject and attribute. An objection that such a middle would itself be a prior subject is answered by distinguishing the subject of an attribute from the subject of a proposition: the middle can be a definition. Five conclusions follow: attributes immediately predicated of their first subject are indemonstrable, while those with a middle are demonstrable; absolute-form attributes are known of their first subject by experience but demonstrable of non-first subjects through it; affirmative connotative attributes are sometimes demonstrable and sometimes not; and negative attributes are demonstrable when their opposite is.
claims: Not every attribute is demonstrable of its first subject: those immediately predicated of it are not.
Attributes signifying an absolute inhering form are known of their first subject by experience, not demonstration.
Some connotative and negative attributes can be demonstrated of their first subject.
